newsitem.title: FRANCE: French capital markets closing report.
newsitem.headline: French capital markets closing report.

text.p: French bond and interest rate futures climbed ahead of the final round of a parliamentary election as investors bought back contracts they had sold earlier, to reduce their exposure in case of post-poll rally, trader said.

The general consensus among market participants was that the left would take power from the ruling centre-right coalition in Sunday's vote but caution prevailed given predictions by pollsters had been unreliable in the previous round, they said.

Traders said the early selling pressure had come predominantly from non-resident funds but this was countered by short covering, mainly from domestic investors, which took the contract higher in the afternoon.

The June bond future settled at 128.52, up 0.38. A surprise win for the right would spark a rally on Monday, even though worries remained about a softening of France's commitment to hitting strict targets for a single European currency.
An outright win for the Socialists, which was not being ruled out by some traders, would be negative but less serious than if the Socialists needed Communist help to take power.

June PIBOR, probably the most sensitive to any poll shocks, also benefitted from the scramble to cover short positions ahead of the weekend vote. It climbed eight basis points to 96.36, narrowing the spread over Euromarks to 44 from 52 on Thursday.

The franc remained stable against the mark at 3.3789 compared with 3.3790 on Thursday. Analysts said a left win would undoubtedly boost near-term volatility. However, the offsetting risks of an EMU delay and a "soft" euro would probably leave the cross relatively stable in the medium term.
The main talking point in the French market on Friday morning was whether the opposition Socialists would have enough seats in the National Assembly to govern without the Communists.

"It depends on the seats, the story in the market today is that maybe the Socialists can win on their own," Philippe Brossard, head of research at ABN Amro Finance said. "The franc would not gain much but it probably wouldn't fall much further."
